teaser: A warship built from thousands of oaks, hauled to the scrapyard by a tug a fraction of her size.
review_notes:
“More than 5,000 oaks” is the commonly quoted figure for the ship's construction.
Sale price £5,530 to John Beatson of Rotherhithe, 1838.
Claim that the masts had already been removed before the tow, that two tugs were used, and that the real hull was black and yellow.
The sun-in-the-wrong-place argument (ship towed west up the Thames, sun set behind her) is the standard reading; worth a check of the wording.
Turner calling the picture “my darling” is a long-repeated tradition.
2005 BBC Radio 4 poll and the 2020 £20 note.

lesson.text: Start with the wood. HMS Temeraire was a warship of 98 guns, and building her swallowed more than 5,000 oak trees. Three gun decks, a crew of several hundred, a hull some 56 meters (185 feet) long. The canvas that remembers her is about 91 by 122 cm (roughly 3 by 4 feet). You could carry it under one arm.

In 1805 she fought at Trafalgar, the sea battle where Britain's navy broke the fleets of France and Spain. When Admiral Nelson's flagship was in trouble, the Temeraire came up beside her and took on two enemy ships at once. Turner's title would later fix the name she is remembered by: the Fighting Temeraire.

Thirty-three years later the navy had no use for her. In 1838 she was sold to a shipbreaker for £5,530, the value of her timber and copper, and towed up the River Thames to be taken apart. Turner was 63. He turned that last trip into a painting, and the two vessels in it could not be more different.

lesson.title: Two ships, two ages
lesson.text: On the left of the picture, a pale giant and a dark little boat travel together. Tap to meet them.

spots.title: The old warship
spots.text: She is painted in creams and golds, almost see-through, like a memory of a ship. Her three masts rise far above everything else on the river.

spots.title: The tug
spots.text: Squat, brown and solid. The rounded box on its side covers a paddle wheel, the churning wheel that pushed early steamboats along.

spots.title: Fire and soot
spots.text: The tall black funnel spits a plume of orange flame and dirty smoke. It drifts back across the warship's masts, staining the clean air she sails in.

spots.title: A white flag
spots.text: A small white flag flies from the tug's mast, higher than the hull of the warship. The Temeraire herself shows no colors at all.

lesson.text: That empty mast mattered to Turner. When he exhibited the picture in 1839, he printed two lines of verse beside it in the catalogue: “The flag which braved the battle and the breeze, / No longer owns her.” A ship without a flag belongs to no one. She is already raw material.

Turner improved on the facts. By the time she was towed, the real Temeraire had been stripped of her masts and was a bare hulk, and her hull was painted black and yellow, not ghostly white. Two tugs did the job, not one.

So this is not a report. It is an elegy, a work made to mourn something. Turner gave the ship her masts back so that you would see what was being lost, then set a sooty machine in front of her so that you would see what was taking her place: steam replacing sail, iron replacing oak.
Turner changed what happened in order to say what it meant. The painting is faithful to a feeling, not to a logbook.

Now turn to the other half of the canvas. The ships take up barely a quarter of the picture. All the rest is sky and water, and the sky is doing as much mourning as the tug's smoke. Two lights share it. One is impossible to miss. The other is easy to overlook.
The sun is going down on the right. Somewhere else in the sky, a second light has already risen. Can you find it?

spots.title: The new moon
spots.text: A thin silver crescent hangs in the cool blue corner, above the ship. One light is leaving and another arrives, just as one kind of ship gives way to another.

lesson.text: The moon's side of the picture is cold: blues, grays, silver. The sun's side burns in orange and red. Turner splits the canvas into two climates, and he puts the old ship in the cool one, as if evening had already reached her. Follow how the picture is built around that split.
Three lines hold this loose-looking picture together.

lines.label: A low horizon
lines.text: The water's edge sits three quarters of the way down. Everything above is sky, which is why the ships look small and the evening looks enormous.

lines.label: The way forward
lines.text: From the warship to the tug to a dark buoy in the corner, the route slides toward you and to the right, into the shadowed water. The journey has one direction.

lines.label: The sun's path
lines.text: The sun drops a column of light straight down the river. It is the brightest warm area in the picture, placed far from the ship, like a door closing at the other end of a room.

lesson.text: Painters and sailors noticed a problem. The Temeraire was towed west, up the Thames toward London. A sun setting in the west should be ahead of her, yet here it blazes off to one side behind the scene. Turner knew the river well. He moved the sun because he needed a sunset more than he needed a compass.

The sky is painted far more thickly than the ships. Turner laid the sunset on in heavy ridges of paint, a technique called impasto, while the Temeraire is brushed in thin, careful layers. Even the texture separates the dying light from the fading ship.

The picture was loved at once, which was not always the case for Turner in his sixties. He refused every offer for it. He is said to have called it “my darling,” and he kept it until he died in 1851, leaving it to the British nation with the rest of his studio.

Britain has kept returning to it. In a 2005 BBC poll, listeners voted it the greatest painting in the country. In 2020 it was printed on the £20 note beside Turner's portrait. Millions of people now carry the old ship's last trip in their wallets.

spots.title: Bare rigging
spots.text: The sails are tightly rolled along the crossbeams. She is not sailing anywhere under her own power, and never will again.

spots.title: A ship under sail
spots.text: Far behind the tug, a small ship with full white sails moves through the blue haze. Sail has not vanished yet, but it is already in the distance.

spots.title: Dark reflections
spots.text: The tug throws a strong brown reflection into the still water. The warship's reflection is pale and faint, as if she weighed nothing.

spots.title: The sun
spots.text: A white disc sinking into red and violet cloud, just above the far bank. Turner keeps it small. The glow around it does the work.

spots.title: The buoy
spots.text: A dark shape bobbing in the gold water, the nearest object to you. It marks the channel, and it is the last stop for your eye in the bottom corner.

spots.title: The burning sky
spots.text: Streaks of orange and yellow fan out from the sun across half the canvas. Stand back and it is cloud. Up close it is thick, dragged paint.

lesson.text: In the 2012 film Skyfall, James Bond sits in front of this painting at the National Gallery in London. A young colleague looks at it and sees a grand old warship being hauled away for scrap. Bond, who is being told he is past his best, says he sees a big ship.

Go back to those 5,000 oaks. Within a year of the tow, the Temeraire was planks and salvaged copper. What survives of her is a few square feet of canvas and a thin layer of oil paint, and it has now lasted far longer than the ship did.

quiz.question: In which battle did the Temeraire earn her fame?
quiz.explanation: She fought beside Nelson's flagship at Trafalgar in 1805.

quiz.question: What is pulling the warship up the river?
options: A steam tug with a paddle wheel
quiz.explanation: A small, dark steam tug tows her, its funnel spitting flame and smoke.

quiz.question: Which of these did Turner change from the real event?
options: He moved the scene to the open sea
He painted the tug larger than the warship
He gave the ship back the masts she had lost
quiz.explanation: The real ship was a mastless hulk by then; Turner restored her masts.

quiz.question: What second light source hides in the upper left of the sky?
quiz.explanation: A thin new moon rises in the cool blue corner while the sun sets on the right.

quiz.question: What did Turner do with the painting after exhibiting it?
options: He sold it to the navy
He cut it into two pictures
He refused to sell it and kept it until his death
quiz.explanation: He turned down every offer and left it to the nation.

quiz.question: How does the paint on the sunset differ from the paint on the ship?
options: It is watercolor instead of oil
It was added by another artist
quiz.explanation: The sky is laid on in thick impasto, while the ship is painted thinly.

facts.text: The Temeraire is flying the British flag in Turner's painting.
facts.explanation: She shows no flag; the only flag is a small white one on the tug.

facts.text: The ship was sold to be broken up for her materials.
facts.explanation: A shipbreaker bought her in 1838 for the value of her timber and copper.

facts.text: The painting is larger than a real ship's sail.
facts.explanation: It measures only about 91 by 122 cm, roughly 3 by 4 feet.
